hints: Notice the question gives the change in force $34 \text{ N}$ and the change in strain $6.0 \times 10^{-5}$, so work with increases in stress and strain rather than total values.
Recall $E = \text{stress}/\text{strain}$ with $\text{stress} = F/A$. Rearrange to $A = F/(E \times \text{strain})$ to find the circular cross-sectional area.
Once $A$ is found, use $A = \pi r^2$ for the wire and take the square root to obtain $r$, checking the final unit is $\text{m}$.
walkthrough: The added weight increases the tensile force by $\Delta F = 34 \text{ N}$ and the tensile strain by $\Delta \text{strain} = 6.0 \times 10^{-5}$. Because the wire obeys Hooke's law, Young modulus links the changes: $E = \Delta \text{stress}/\Delta \text{strain}$.
First find the increase in stress: $\Delta \text{stress} = E \times \Delta \text{strain} = (2.5 \times 10^{11}) \times (6.0 \times 10^{-5}) = 1.5 \times 10^{7} \text{ Pa}$.
Stress is force per area, so $\Delta \text{stress} = \Delta F/A$. Rearrange for area: $A = \Delta F/\Delta \text{stress} = 34/(1.5 \times 10^{7}) \approx 2.27 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$.
For circular cross-section $A = \pi r^2$, so $r = \sqrt{A/\pi} = \sqrt{2.27 \times 10^{-6}/\pi} \approx \sqrt{7.21 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 8.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$.
